3n1qd2: This week there is no new grammar. It's a stop to organize what you already know: with these pieces you can already have your first complete conversation in Spanish. Each summary ends with the most frequent mix-ups at this point in the course.
1fupcgz: With **ser** you say who you are: your name (**Soy Nadia**), your origin (**Soy de Malabo**), your nationality (**Soy ecuatoguineana**), and your profession (**Soy diseñadora**). It's the verb of identity.
842g42: Origin and nationality say the same thing with two structures: **ser de + place** (soy de Chile) or **ser + adjective** (soy chileno, soy chilena). Don't mix the two: _soy de chilena_ doesn't exist.
1ppleit: With a profession no article is used: **Soy enfermera**, not _soy una enfermera_. The article appears only if you add more information: _Es una enfermera muy buena_.
ijsaw9: Remember the plural forms: **somos**, **sois** (vosotros, only in Spain), and **son** (ellos, ellas, ustedes). In Latin America, to address a group, **ustedes** is always used, even among friends.
1m8jamz: If you hesitate between _de + country_ and the nationality, use **ser de**: _Soy de Corea_ is always correct, even if you don't remember the adjective.
1im73rw: With _ser_ + profession no article is used.
1cjz2bd: _Nosotros_ goes with **somos**; _son_ is for ellos, ellas, and ustedes.
m3ben5: Things: gender, plural, articles, and hay
t3q86: All nouns have gender. Many in **-o** are masculine (el libro) and many in **-a** are feminine (la mesa), but there are frequent exceptions: **el día**, **el mapa**, **el idioma**, **el problema**, **la mano**, **la foto**. Words in **-e** or in a consonant must be learned with their article: **la clase**, **el lápiz**.
83moz6: Plural: vowel + **-s** (mesa → mesas), consonant + **-es** (papel → papeles), and **z → ces** (lápiz → lápices).
18hf4sn: **El, la, los, las** talk about something known or unique: _el teléfono de Rocío_. **Un, una, unos, unas** introduce something new: _un teléfono_.
1s8gymq: **Hay** says that something exists in a place. It's one single form for singular and plural, and goes with **un/una**, with numbers, or without an article: _Hay una impresora_, _Hay doce mesas_, _Hay café_. It never goes with _el, la, los, las_.
ui05k1: Ordenador (Spain) and computadora (Latin America) are the same thing. Use the word from the region you prefer, but recognize both.
2cn18u: _Hay_ introduces something new: it goes with **un/una**, never with _el/la_.
8u7pn0: _Problema_ is masculine even though it ends in -a.
sx4okc: To talk about what you do, you use regular verbs in **-ar**: you remove **-ar** and add the ending for the person: habl**o**, habl**as**, habl**a**, habl**amos**, habl**áis**, habl**an**. It's the same with trabajar, estudiar, dedicarse, necesitar, or escuchar.
1ac8rpk: To negate, put **no** right before the verb: **No hablo francés**. If you answer a question, there are often two _no_: **—¿Trabajas aquí? —No, no trabajo aquí.** The first answers; the second negates the verb.
14t68zl: Question words take an accent mark: **qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, quién, cuánto**. They go at the beginning, right before the verb: **¿Dónde trabajas?** In yes/no questions there's no special word: the intonation rises at the end: **¿Hablas inglés?**
1a56ojm: In a question, _dónde_ takes an accent mark.
13r3lad: After the question word comes the verb; the pronoun is normally left out.
h6yv6w: An introduction sounds natural when the sentences are connected: **y** adds (hablo inglés **y** francés), **pero** contrasts (soy ingeniera, **pero** ahora estudio diseño), and **también** adds something equal (Pau es estudiante; Nadia **también**).
1f75hud: Before a word that begins with the sound **i**, _y_ changes to **e**: **español e inglés**.
1jpbad: Numbers: from 16 to 29 they are written as one word (**dieciséis, veintidós, veintiocho**); from 31 on they are written as three (**treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco**). **Cien** is exactly 100.
v3bgdp: Phone numbers are often said in groups of two digits: 99 23 45 80 → **noventa y nueve, veintitrés, cuarenta y cinco, ochenta**. If you don't understand, ask for clarification: **¿Cómo? Más despacio, por favor.**
fppu9c: To sound natural in an introduction, use at least one **pero** and one **también**: they are the difference between a list and a text.

1efhhn8: Review: vowels, syllables, stress, and intonation
gty1q1: The four weeks of pronunciation form a system. There are five **vowels** and they are always clear. Each **syllable** has about the same duration: Spanish sounds like a regular train, ta-ta-ta-ta. One of those syllables is stronger: the **stress**. And the **intonation** of the sentence says whether you are asking or stating.
wnuzpn: If you change the stress, you sometimes change the word: **trabajo** (yo, now) versus **trabajó** (in the past, you'll see it later). And if you change the intonation, you change the message: **Eres de Chile.** (you state) versus **¿Eres de Chile?** (you ask, the voice rises at the end).
181bjxs: In questions with **qué, dónde, cómo**, the voice normally falls at the end: the question word already says it's a question.
e2qr2g: The written accent mark marks the strong syllable when it doesn't follow the general rule (**teléfono**, **lápiz**) and also distinguishes the question words: **¿dónde?** versus _donde_.
1grf4jg: Ar-qui-tec-ta: four full vowels. Don't say «arquitect-uh».
hb447n: The question rises at the end ↗; the answer falls ↘.
1v58dfg: Questions with a question word: start high on _dónde_ / _qué_ and fall at the end.
mk1406: Mark the strong syllable with a hand beat: te-**lé**, **nú**-me, cua-**der**, or-de-na-**dor**, **lá**-piz.
